Being Left Out

When other children say “You're not allowed to play”: this story helps make sense of the sting of exclusion and find a way back in.

A personalized picture book in which your child is the hero — and masters this challenge themselves. The first story is free.

Create This Story

At recess, three children are playing tag, and when your child wants to join, the sentence comes that hurts so much: “You're not allowed to play.” Maybe your child mentions it casually over the afternoon snack, maybe nothing comes out at all, just a quiet face and a “today was just stupid.” You'd love nothing more than to march onto the playground yourself — and know you can't. What's left is how to help your child now, without making the situation bigger than it is.

What's happening is usually not planned cruelty, but the testing of group belonging that begins at this age. Children try out who “belongs” and who doesn't, often without realizing how much force the sentence carries — empathy for someone outside your own group is still growing between roughly four and eight. For the excluded child, the moment still feels enormous: belonging is closely tied to a child's own sense of worth, and a “no” lands hard. One distinction matters: a single scene forgotten by tomorrow differs from a pattern that targets the same child week after week.

A story gives this painful moment words your child often can't find yet. It shows a character living through exactly this exclusion, seen from outside — the feeling can be looked at instead of only being raw and overwhelming. Because the character finds a way to handle the disappointment and seek new connection, some of that confidence carries over: being excluded is not the end, just a moment that passes. And because the book can be reopened whenever needed, your child can return to it right when the next playground moment stings.

In the personalized story, your child — with their own face on every page — experiences what exclusion feels like, and finds their way back into play step by step: through another child, a new offer, sometimes simply through time passing. The story stays honest about the feeling of rejection, but also shows that friendships shift, and that a “no” from one group often leads to a “yes” somewhere else. The first personalized story is free to try, so you can check without commitment whether it fits your child's current situation.

Listen without immediately judging or solving the situation — often “that hurts, I understand” is enough as a first step. Ask whether it was a one-off or whether the same child is repeatedly excluded; the latter is a signal to talk to the teacher. Practise simple sentences together for next time, like “Can I play with you later?”, and encourage your child to approach other children too, rather than only one group. If your child withdraws for weeks, avoids the playground entirely, or seems persistently sad, a conversation with the school or a child psychologist is worthwhile.

What your child learns

Emotional resilience, self-worth, seeking new connections, naming feelings, perspective.

Recommended age

4-8 years

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I react when my child says they weren't allowed to play?

First just listen and name the feeling, instead of immediately offering a solution — “that hurts, I understand” is often enough as a first step. Then calmly ask what exactly happened, without jumping to judge the other side. Only after that do you think together about what your child could try next.

Is a single instance of exclusion already bullying?

Not necessarily — a single scene forgotten by tomorrow is often part of the normal testing of group belonging among children. Bullying is more likely when the same child is targeted for exclusion again and again, over a longer period. If the pattern repeats, a conversation with the school makes sense.

Should I talk to the teacher if my child is being left out?

For a one-off incident, an attentive ear at home is usually enough. But if the exclusion repeats over weeks or always involves the same group, a matter-of-fact conversation with the teacher is worthwhile — they often see the group dynamics from a different angle than you do.

How do I rebuild my child's self-worth after such an experience?

Emphasize that a “no” from one group says nothing about your child's worth, and is often simply a snapshot of that moment. Remind them of other situations where they did find connection, and encourage them to approach other children too. Time and repeated good experiences work more powerfully here than a single conversation.

How can a story help with dealing with exclusion?

It gives the painful moment a shape your child can look at from the outside, instead of only experiencing it raw. In the personalized version, your child lives through exactly this situation with their own face, and sees how a way back into play opens up again after exclusion.
